strengths: Addresses an important and practical gap in multivariate time series forecasting: channel-wise asynchronous sampling, test-time block-wise missingness, and inter-channel dependencies under a unified problem formulation.

Proposes ChannelTokenFormer, a technically plausible Transformer-based framework that uses channel tokens, frequency-adaptive patching, unified masked attention, and read-only cross-channel communication to handle variable-length and partially observed inputs without relying on interpolation.

Provides extensive experiments across four datasets, including a real-world LNG cargo handling system dataset, seven representative baselines, two practical scenarios, varying missing ratios, multiple ablations, error bars, input-length robustness tests, and frequency-domain analysis.

Ablation studies support the utility of key components, especially patch masking, and the method consistently performs well under increasing test-time missingness, where the advantages over interpolation/zero-fill baselines are most visible.
The paper is generally well organized, with detailed appendices covering dataset construction, implementation details, additional ablations, and full results.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the main contributions combine existing ideas such as variate/channel tokens, FFT-based adaptive patching, masked attention, and random patch masking. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its technical novelty from prior irregular-sampling, missing-value, and patch-based forecasting work.

The baseline suite lacks specialized methods for irregular/asynchronous and missing-value forecasting, such as BRITS, GRU-D, SERT, ContiFormer, mTAND, or GraFIT. Baselines are mostly regular forecasting models adapted via interpolation or zero-filling, so the central claims about robustness to asynchrony and missingness are not fully validated against the most relevant prior art.

Evaluation relies heavily on modified benchmark datasets whose construction is somewhat ad hoc and may not reflect real-world channel dependencies or missingness distributions. The real-world CHS dataset is proprietary, uses only 10 selected channels, and is not publicly released, limiting reproducibility.

Some technical and implementation details are underspecified, including the threshold for 'strong' dominant frequency, how partially missing patches are handled (as opposed to fully missing patches), how hyperparameters such as channel-token count and random masking ratio are selected, and whether model selection uses validation data consistently.

Improvements over strong baselines are marginal on some datasets and in the conventional setting. The paper also acknowledges quadratic attention scalability issues but provides no efficiency or memory analysis, which is important for real-world high-dimensional forecasting.

strengths: Targets an important and under-explored practical forecasting setting: channel-wise asynchronous sampling and block-wise test-time missingness.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is architecturally reasonable, combining channel tokens, read-only cross-channel attention, frequency-adaptive patching, and patch masking in a unified Transformer framework.
The paper includes experiments on multiple modified benchmark datasets and a real-world LNG cargo handling dataset, with ablations and some error bars.
The motivation analysis of interpolation-induced spectral distortion is useful and clearly presented in the appendix.
The problem formulation explicitly accounts for heterogeneous sampling periods and missingness masks, which is a useful step toward more realistic forecasting benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method largely combines existing ideas such as global/channel tokens, read-only/prompt attention, FFT-based patching, and patch masking/dropout. No fundamentally new technical contribution is demonstrated.

Evaluation is not competitive for a top-tier venue because the baselines are standard regular-sampling forecasters that are forced to use interpolation or zero-filling. The paper does not compare against irregularly sampled, asynchronous, or missing-value-aware forecasting methods (e.g., mTAND, ContiFormer, SeFT, RAINDROP, BRITS, GRU-D, SERT), despite discussing them in related work.

The test-time missingness evaluation is biased toward the proposed model: baselines receive zero-filled missing values, while ChannelTokenFormer uses a binary mask to exclude fully missing patches. A simple imputation-plus-forecasting baseline could be much stronger but is not evaluated.

The proposed missingness mechanism only handles fully missing patches aligned with patch boundaries; partial missing patches are not addressed, and the SolarWind evaluation is constructed so that missing blocks span exactly one patch length. Robustness to arbitrary block lengths and partial gaps is not convincingly established.

The modified benchmark datasets are created by arbitrary resampling/grouping of channels, and there is no sensitivity analysis showing that conclusions hold under different asynchronous sampling configurations. The real-world CHS dataset uses only 10 selected channels and is not clearly released, limiting reproducibility.

Empirical gains are often marginal and may be within variance. For example, in Table 1, CHS CMSE is 0.282 for CTF vs. 0.286 for CrossGNN, and CMAE is 0.126 vs. 0.128, which does not support strong claims of superior robustness and accuracy.

The central claim that all three challenges—dependency, asynchrony, and missingness—must be addressed in a unified framework is not rigorously justified. The ablations show degradations when components are removed, but do not compare against alternative simple modular solutions or strong baselines adapted to the setting.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or model release is mentioned, the industrial dataset appears proprietary, and tuning details for some baselines and the modified datasets are insufficient for exact replication.

Scalability and computational cost are acknowledged as limitations but not analyzed. Since the model applies full attention across all local and channel tokens, the claimed parameter efficiency is not supported with complexity or runtime measurements.

The evaluation metric CMSE/CMAE changes the forecasting problem by evaluating channels over different future step counts after resampling. This may obscure practical utility, and its comparability to standard forecasting metrics is not fully established.
The conventional-setting results in Table 11 are poorly formatted and appear inconsistent, weakening the claim that the model also performs well in standard multivariate forecasting.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored practical problem: channel-wise asynchronous sampling, inter-channel dependencies, and block-wise test-time missing intervals in multivariate time series forecasting.
Provides a clear problem formulation with variable prediction horizons per channel and channel-aggregated metrics (CMSE/CMAE), which is useful for evaluating models under asynchronous sampling.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is technically plausible: channel tokens, frequency-adaptive patching, masked unified attention, and patch-level masking jointly support variable-length and missing inputs.

The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including three modified benchmarks and a real-world LNG cargo handling system dataset, with comparisons against several representative forecasting baselines.
The empirical results consistently show advantages over adapted standard baselines, especially under increasing test-time missing ratios, and ablations support the utility of the main components.
The paper includes useful additional analyses on attention masking strategies, channel token count, robustness to input length variability, and frequency-domain behavior.
The manuscript is generally well organized, with substantial implementation and dataset details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The baseline set does not include methods explicitly designed for irregularly sampled time series or missing-value-aware forecasting (e.g., BRITS, GRU-D, Raindrop, mTAND, SeFT, ContiFormer, SERT). Since the paper's central claims concern asynchrony and missingness, comparisons to aligned models adapted via interpolation/zero-filling are not sufficient to establish robustness against the strongest relevant alternatives.

The practical benchmark settings are mostly custom modifications of standard datasets. The construction of ETT1-practical, Weather-practical, and SolarWind-practical may unintentionally favor interpolation-free modeling, and the paper does not provide sufficient sensitivity analysis to rule out this concern.

The comparison pipeline is potentially asymmetric: ChannelTokenFormer can explicitly exclude forward-filled or missing values, while baselines are trained/tested with interpolation or zero-filling. This makes the performance gaps harder to interpret, even if all models are evaluated on the same ground-truth targets.

The frequency-domain analysis is limited to the ETT1 dataset and a single interpolation-based baseline (TimeXer). The spectral fidelity gains are small in several metrics, and stronger empirical evidence is needed to support broad claims about preventing interpolation-induced distortion.

Scalability is acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically studied. Attention over all local and channel tokens is quadratic in the total token count, and there is no runtime, memory, or scaling analysis as the number of channels increases.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model checkpoints are provided, the modified datasets and generation scripts are not clearly available, and the real-world CHS dataset appears proprietary, making independent verification difficult.

The main paper reports averaged results without significance tests, while error bars are largely relegated to the appendix. This weakens confidence that some of the smaller improvements are statistically meaningful.

Ablations are mainly conducted on the SolarWind dataset, and some component removals produce relatively modest degradation. Cross-dataset ablations would better support the claim that dependency, dynamic patching, and masking are broadly necessary.

Some design choices, such as the number of channel tokens and FFT-based patch lengths, are tuned per dataset. This is reasonable, but it raises concerns about generalization and potential overfitting to the proposed practical settings.
The setting assumes the forecast horizon is fully observed and focuses only on input missingness. This limits the generality of the robustness claims for real-world deployment.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored combination of challenges in multivariate forecasting: channel-wise asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness, and cross-channel dependencies, which prior work largely treats in isolation.

Proposes a unified and reasonably elegant framework (ChannelTokenFormer) that avoids interpolation by using channel tokens, frequency-based dynamic patching, and mask-guided attention, with an explicit training-time proxy for test-time missing blocks.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation across four adapted public benchmarks and two real-world/industrial datasets, including robustness tests under varying missing ratios and input lengths, plus scalability and ablation studies.
Includes a useful frequency-domain analysis showing how interpolation can induce spectral distortion (amplitude attenuation, phase delay, leakage), which helps motivate the interpolation-free design.
The method is well motivated and clearly described, with implementation details, hyperparameters, error bars over multiple seeds, and a reproducibility/ethics statement.

Demonstrates competitive or best performance in many settings, with ablations showing that channel dependence, dynamic patching, and masking each contribute, and the unified attention design is parameter-efficient compared with separate modules.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: channel tokens, FFT-guided patching, patch masking, and read-only attention masking all have precedents (e.g., iTransformer, TimeXer, PatchDropout, read-only prompt attention); the main contribution is their combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The practical benchmarks are constructed by resampling standard datasets to create asynchronous sampling, which may not fully reflect real-world asynchrony; the private CHS dataset is also not publicly available, limiting external verification.

Performance gains are generally modest and not uniformly dominant: CTF is sometimes tied or slightly worse than baselines on individual metrics (e.g., CMAE on CHS, CMSE on Weather, ETT2 comparison with modified TimeXer), and some ablation differences are small.

The evaluation protocol defines channel-specific forecast horizons and CMSE/CMAE aggregation, which is non-standard and may limit direct comparability with prior multivariate forecasting results; it also changes the effective task definition.

Baseline handling of asynchronous inputs relies on interpolation, which may disadvantage regular baselines; although a modified TimeXer is included, the comparison does not fully isolate interpolation effects from architecture differences, and some baselines are reimplemented rather than run from official code.

Missingness handling assumes block-wise missing values in the input and only fully unobserved patches are removed; behavior for partially missing patches, arbitrary missing block lengths misaligned with patch boundaries, or missingness in the target horizon is not fully specified.

Scalability is limited by quadratic attention: OOM occurs at 280 channels on a single 24GB GPU, and memory grows linearly with input length, which may restrict use in very high-dimensional or long-context industrial settings.
The number of channel tokens is manually selected per dataset (1–3) and the FFT threshold/fallback requires tuning; there is no automatic selection procedure or detailed sensitivity analysis.

Claims of robustness and superiority are supported mainly by empirical results on adapted benchmarks; there is no formal theoretical guarantee for the unified attention/masking design, and statistical significance testing is not reported beyond seed-based error bars.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem setting that combines channel-wise asynchronous sampling, test-time block-wise missingness, and cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time series forecasting.

Proposes a coherent Transformer-based framework, ChannelTokenFormer, with several reasonable design choices: channel tokens, frequency-guided dynamic patching, mask-guided attention, and random patch masking as a training proxy for missingness.

Provides a relatively extensive empirical study across adapted benchmark datasets and one private industrial LNG dataset, including comparisons with channel-dependent, channel-independent, irregular-sampling, and missing-aware baselines.

Includes useful additional analyses such as ablations, channel-token count sensitivity, input-length robustness, scalability, and a frequency-domain comparison, and provides reproducibility and ethics statements.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and largely incremental: the method combines existing ideas such as channel tokens from iTransformer/TimeXer, FFT-based patching from time-series foundation models, PatchDropout-style masking, and read-only attention. The unified mask-guided attention is mostly an engineering composition rather than a fundamental conceptual advance.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. The 'practical' datasets are synthetically resampled in ad hoc ways, and the comparison may be unfair because regular baselines must rely on interpolation while CTF operates on non-interpolated inputs and receives explicit missingness masks at test time. The private industrial dataset cannot be verified.

Several main-result improvements are marginal, e.g., Weather and some ETT2 cases, and the main paper tables lack error bars despite variance being reported only in the appendix. Claims of 'superior robustness' and 'consistently outperforming' are therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

The missingness handling assumes test-time missing masks are known and provided to the model, which is a strong and often unrealistic assumption in real-world deployment. The ablation shows patch masking yields only small gains except under severe missingness, weakening the claimed centrality of this component.

Dynamic patching relies on heuristic FFT peak detection with a fixed percentile threshold and fallback rules, but there is little sensitivity analysis or justification for these choices. It is unclear how robust this mechanism is across datasets with weak or noisy periodicity.

The unified attention masking strategy is not convincingly shown to be necessary: some ablations show near-identical performance among variants (e.g., CD-ReadOnly vs. CD-ReadOnly-Indexed), and the frequency-bias analysis reports very small RMSE differences that may not support the strength of the conclusions.

Presentation and reproducibility issues reduce confidence: several tables are malformed or contain typos/inconsistent baseline names, some baselines are reimplemented or approximated (e.g., ContiFormer ODE solver), and code is not yet available for inspection.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored combination of practical challenges: channel-wise asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness, and cross-channel dependencies.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is technically coherent: channel tokens summarize per-channel information, frequency-guided dynamic patching avoids forcing a common resolution, and mask-guided attention handles variable token counts and missing patches without interpolation.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, covering multiple adapted benchmarks, one private industrial dataset, numerous baselines across channel-dependent, channel-independent, irregular, and missing-aware models, multiple prediction horizons, missing ratios, ablations, scalability tests, and frequency-domain analysis.
The problem formulation and channel-aggregated metrics (CMSE/CMAE) are appropriate for asynchronous channels with different valid prediction lengths.
Ablations support the contribution of the main components, and the comparison to a modified TimeXer helps isolate interpolation-induced distortion from architectural effects.
Reproducibility is generally well addressed through detailed hyperparameters, data-source descriptions, and a promise to release code.
The paper is clearly written and well motivated, with useful practical framing and good visualization of the proposed masking strategies and forecasting behavior.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing ideas such as channel tokens from iTransformer/TimeXer, frequency-guided patching from foundation models, PatchDropout-style masking, and read-only attention. The unified masking design is useful but not deeply novel or theoretically justified.

Evaluation relies heavily on synthetically modified benchmark datasets, where asynchrony and missingness are injected by resampling or assigning sampling periods. This limits evidence that the method generalizes to naturally occurring real-world asynchrony, and only one private dataset is used for real-world validation.

The method assumes that reliable test-time binary missingness masks are available at inference. In many practical settings, missing indicators may be unavailable, noisy, or not aligned with patch boundaries, and the assumption that the forecast horizon is fully observed may be optimistic.

Some baseline comparisons may be unfair or approximate: regular baselines are trained/evaluated after interpolation, irregular baselines are reimplemented in a common framework, and ContiFormer is approximated rather than run faithfully.

Performance gains are sometimes marginal (e.g., Weather, ETT2, and the frequency-domain RMSE differences), and statistical significance is not consistently reported. For CHS, the CMAE of iPatchGNN is slightly better than CTF, contradicting the broad claim of best performance on all datasets.

Frequency-based dynamic patching depends on heuristic choices such as a 70th-percentile FFT threshold and a fallback rule. The sensitivity and robustness of these choices are not sufficiently explored.

Scalability remains limited by quadratic attention over tokens/channels; the method scales to hundreds of channels but incurs high memory and OOM at 280 channels, which may restrict very high-dimensional applications.

The attention mechanism is not fully analyzed: local tokens cannot attend to channel tokens, so the effect of global channel-token information on local representations is indirect. More analysis of learned channel interactions and attention behavior would strengthen the paper.
